Chapter 7: The Ongoing Need for Empathy—Beyond the Crisis.
As time goes by and the dust settles after a crisis, it’s natural for the world to move on. But if you’re living with cancer or have come through treatment, this period can feel surprisingly lonely.
Remember those early days? The steady stream of cards, casseroles, and check-in texts? They start to fade, and suddenly, that circle of support feels a whole lot smaller. But here’s the thing—the need for empathy doesn’t just disappear.
Take the story of a man in his sixties. When he was in the thick of treatment, he was surrounded by friends. But once it was over, the silence set in. People figured he must be “better” now, that he didn’t need company or help anymore. But in reality, he’d never felt more isolated. That fear of the cancer coming back still lingered, and the emotional scars were painfully fresh.
Most folks don’t realize that sometimes, the hardest part comes after the treatments are finished. The adrenaline of simply surviving gives way to the slow, steady work of rebuilding. There are still doctor appointments, scans, and that constant, nagging worry—what if something’s wrong? While the world expects you to just be grateful, what you really need is understanding.
Or think about a young mother, back at work after a whole year of treatment. She wanted to prove she was capable, but the fatigue hit her like a wave. Her colleagues were eager to move on, and they stopped asking how she was doing. She missed the little things—a cup of tea, a listening ear—gestures that had meant everything during the toughest days.
Here’s something we don’t talk about enough: empathy isn’t just for the crisis. It’s for the long haul. It’s the friend who keeps checking in, months later. The family member who remembers the anniversary of the diagnosis. The coworker who quietly covers a shift when you’re too tired to make it in. These small acts quietly say, “I haven’t forgotten. I’m still here.”
Over time, people living with cancer learn how to speak up for themselves. They get braver about asking for what they need, even when it feels awkward. They remind those around them that healing isn’t a finish line—it’s a process. And along the way, they discover just how rare and precious true empathy can be.
So, here’s the key takeaway: support shouldn’t end when the crisis does. The need for kindness, patience, and real understanding? It’s still there. If you care about someone on this journey, the most important thing you can do is keep showing up. Keep listening. And remember—the journey isn’t over yet.
